item: The Looking around chapter (pan, turn, tilt, zoom, home)
why: Turn and tilt are keyboard-only on desktop, and the chapter holds back the housing, seats and money chapters. Players kept it open 150 weeks on average.
now: Early in year 1, the objectives drawer opens a chapter called Looking around. It asks the player to pan the map, turn the view, tilt the view and zoom, and to go back home optionally. The next chapters (Somewhere to sleep, then Seats and Paying for it) don't open until it's done. On a touch screen there are buttons for turn and tilt. On desktop there are none: the only way is the Q/E and Z/X keys, which the chapter's help text mentions but nothing on screen shows.
change: Remove this chapter, so the chain goes straight from the second course to housing. The camera is then learned by using it, with the turn, tilt and home buttons shown on desktop too. The review found a player who never guessed the keys was stuck here all year, never got the housing chapter, and reached year 2 with fewer students than they started with. You chose to keep the chapter and add a skip button; Plan 124 does that, and also shows the turn and tilt buttons on desktop, because their absence is a bug either way.

item: The map tools' help (?): one 280-word paragraph of keys and touch tips
who: anyone who opens the map tools
why: Once turn, tilt and home are buttons on desktop too, the keys can be a short list on the buttons' own hovers.
now: When you open the map tools (the button at the bottom right of the map), a (?) help sits beside the zoom buttons. It is one paragraph of about 280 words. It covers how to build, rotate, draw paths and plant trees, every keyboard shortcut, and how touch screens work.
change: Shorten it to the few things that belong next to the map tools: the camera keys as a short list, one line on building and one on paths. The touch-screen sentences would show only on touch screens. Building instructions the Build menu already gives would go.

item: Year-1 chapter 'about' paragraphs (next course, sleep, seats, paying, first summer, standing)
why: In the silent run the objective line beside each carried the run. From the fifth chapter, half the briefings are never opened and the chapters still get done.
now: Each chapter in the objectives drawer has a short paragraph under its title explaining the rules behind it. For example: how long a course takes to write, that each course adds 80 class places, how money comes in and goes out, what prestige and satisfaction are. Below the paragraph are the objectives themselves ("Start a program's second course" and so on).
change: Delete the paragraph for the six year-1 chapters and keep the objective lines. In the silent run the objective lines alone were enough. Play statistics show that from the fifth chapter on, about half of players never open the briefing, yet still finish the chapter.

item: The 'why you can't yet' help variants (second course waiting, hall unaffordable, lab rising)
why: They exist because objectives open before their control is lit. Gate the objective instead.
now: Some objectives appear before the player can possibly do them, so the game adds a help text explaining the wait. Examples: "start the second course" while the first course still has 4 weeks to go; "place an academic hall" about 40 weeks before it's affordable; "move a program into it" while the hall is still being built.
change: Change the rule instead of explaining it: an objective only appears once its button can actually be pressed. Then the three 'why you can't yet' helps can be deleted. Where waiting is the lesson, the button itself can show progress, for example the hall's card filling up as cash approaches its price.

item: The four tab walks (Treasury, Students, History, Faculty) and their 'Walk through…' objectives
why: Silent, each is a title and Next three times. The Treasury walk is 258 words for one click, the worst ratio of year 1.
now: Four short guided tours, one each for the Treasury, Students, History and Faculty tabs. Each is two or three cards that point at parts of the tab, with a Next button, and each is a chapter objective ("Walk through the Treasury tab"). The Treasury tour is about 258 words.
change: Remove the four tours and their objectives. With the text hidden, each tour was just a title and Next three times, and the tabs' own labels were enough to make every decision. The Treasury tour was the most reading per click in the whole first year.

item: The admissions coach (six tips) and the handle hint
why: The admissions screen played perfectly with no text. It is the game's best teaching surface.
now: At the first summer's admissions page, a coach shows six tips one after another (set the price first, what the dots mean, drag the handle to raise the bar, and so on). A separate hint under the handle says to drag it.
change: Remove the coach and the hint, and keep the admissions page exactly as it is. Played with no text at all, the page taught itself. The price verdict, the applicant dots, the hall filling up and the 'What this class does' panel carried every decision. It is the best-teaching screen in the game.

item: The first summer's chapter text and the summer call's 53-word note
why: The note is already on screen with a sun and one button.
now: When the first summer arrives, its chapter has a 53-word paragraph explaining that the clock has stopped, where the summer note is, and what the summer's three pages are. The note at the bottom left also has its own text.
change: Remove that paragraph and trim the note's text. The note is already on screen with a sun and one button to open the summer, which says the same thing.

item: Summer review lines explaining satisfaction and the four 'X stands at N of 150' pillar lines
why: The header shows satisfaction the next moment; the pillars become one figure (card 7).
now: At each summer, the year in review explains what satisfaction is ("how happy your students are, out of 100…"). It also has four lines like "Academics stands at 62 of 150, and counts for 40%", one per pillar.
change: Remove the satisfaction explanation (the header shows the number a moment later) and the four pillar sentences (the report card's bars just above show the same thing).

item: 'The cost of being large' note shown from year 1
why: It is about colleges past about 1,500 students. Show it only then.
now: The Treasury tab shows a note called 'The cost of being large' from the very first year. It explains that running costs rise once a college grows past about 1,500 students.
change: Recommended: show it only once the college is near that size, since it means nothing to a 350-student college. You chose to cut the note entirely; the cost itself stays in the Treasury's figures.

item: The founding letter 'The doors open' (70 words) and the second panel at the first placement
why: It covers the payoff of the founding: the hall the player just designed.
now: After the founding form, the player clicks 'Open the doors'. The screen cuts to an empty wooded site with a 70-word letter titled 'The doors open'. When the player then places Founders Hall, the hall pops in at full size and two text panels open at once.
change: Remove the letter, start straight on the empty plot with the hall ready to place, and show one panel after placement instead of two. (Separately, the review suggested making the hall rise into place, which isn't a cut.)

item: Small redundant lines: 'A run lasts 50 years…', 'The walkthrough has two steps.', 'Time is paused until you do this'
why: The screen already says each one.
now: Three small lines in the opening: 'A run lasts 50 years. At the end of Year 50 the board writes your Final Report…'; 'The walkthrough has two steps.'; and 'Time is paused until you do this'.
change: Delete them. The title screen already says 'Fifty years to build a university', the cards already say Step one and Step two, and the clock visibly shows it's paused.

item: The 'unseen' red ! badges on Curriculum, Build and each Build category
why: Seven of eight Build categories carry one at year 30, and the same red marks Athletics' real problem.
now: A small red '!' badge appears on the Curriculum button, the Build button and each category inside the Build menu whenever something new has unlocked that you haven't looked at. By year 30, seven of the eight Build categories carry one. The same red '!' on Athletics means something different: a team is missing staff.
change: Remove the 'something new' badges, so the only badge left means 'this needs you' (like Athletics' missing staff). Draw that one so it shows clearly on any school colour. You chose trim; Plan 124 removes the badges on each Build category and keeps the two on the toolbar buttons.

item: The drawer's 'Also waiting' section and the toast for a pending matter
why: One pending decision shows in five places. Keep the Inbox badge and NEXT.
now: When a matter in the Inbox needs a decision, it shows in five places at once: the ticker's NEXT line, the red count on the Inbox button, an 'Also waiting' section in the objectives drawer, a 'This week' pill on the Inbox row, and a toast that slides in.
change: Remove the drawer's 'Also waiting' section and the toast for matters, leaving the Inbox badge and NEXT. Fewer repeats mean the remaining ones stand out.

item: Athletics' six 'Hire a … →' links that repeat the chapter step
why: The chapter chip and the lit target already say it.
now: When the Athletics chapter asks you to staff teams, the Athletics tab shows six underlined links like 'Hire a head coach →', one per missing post. The same step is also on the chapter chip, in the drawer, and as a '!' on the Athletics button.
change: Remove the six links and let the chapter chip and the highlighted target carry the step. The links also look different from every other tab's buttons.

item: Four date readouts (calendar card, 'Year 16', weekday pips, ticker stamp)
why: One calendar card: YEAR 16 · FALL · 2.
now: The date shows four ways on the top band: the calendar card (FALL / 2 / WEEK), 'Year 16', the row of weekday pips, and a 'Y16W1' stamp on the ticker.
change: Merge them into one calendar card that says YEAR 16 · FALL · WEEK 2, and drop the duplicates.

item: Separate Rank and Prestige chips
why: Rank follows from prestige, and both open History. One chip: #48 · 64.8, with the pillar bars of card 7.
now: The top band has a Rank chip (#48) and a Prestige chip (64.8) side by side. Rank comes directly from prestige, and both open the History tab.
change: Merge them into one chip reading '#48 · 64.8'. You chose trim; Plan 124 keeps both chips but gives them one shared hint and one destination.

item: 'X is now an established program' letters
saves: ≈ −5 letters a year mid-game, ≈ −120 words a year
why: The hall's silver ring and the chime are the event. Five of six year-15 Inbox items were these.
now: Mid-game, whenever a program reaches 'established' standing, a letter arrives saying so. At year 15, five of the six items in the Inbox were these letters. The program's hall also gets a silver ring on the map and a chime plays.
change: Stop sending these letters: the ring on the hall and the chime are the announcement. About five fewer letters a year.

item: Faculty tiles' 'N WAITING' and the satisfaction sub-lines ('A need since…', beds wanted)
saves: ≈ −12 words a tile row, ≈ −30 on Students
why: Once the map shows unlit windows and queues (card 8), the words repeat it.
now: Faculty cards show '8 WAITING' (courses that need a teacher). The Students tab has sub-lines under each need, such as 'A need since the college passed 1,500 students' or '9,390 beds, 5,655 wanted'.
change: Once the map shows these things (a dark window on a hall for each course with no teacher, a queue at a building that's short), shorten or drop the words. You chose trim; Plan 124 keeps the count as a number with an icon and drops the 'since when' lines.

item: Promises (the summer offer, the Promises panel, 2,300 words)
why: Weak one-off effects; the championships player takes none and finishes 14th; 11 players opened its chapter.
now: From the summer review, the board offers a promise: a target by a deadline, such as a rank, a size, or founding a school. Kept or missed, it gives small rewards or penalties (alumni warmth, satisfaction, a little money), and the Final Report lists them. It has its own panel in History and about 2,300 words of text.
change: Remove promises entirely. The effects are small one-offs that no other system depends on. The championships player never took one and still finished 14th, and few players opened the promises chapter.

item: Student demands (fold the deadline into satisfaction's drag, which the header already names)
why: A weak bump to a stock that halves in 14 weeks; the header chip already names the need.
now: When satisfaction drops below a threshold, students raise a demand (for example more dining) with a deadline. Meeting or missing it gives a small bump to satisfaction. It appears as a card and in the Inbox.
change: Remove demands as a separate system. The header's satisfaction chip already names the need that's dragging it down, and the bump fades by half in about 14 weeks.

item: Identity tags' teeth (keep the tags as words in the guidebook and Final Report)
why: ±2–12% on an applicant pool that seat-bound colleges do not need.
now: The college earns identity tags over the years (research-heavy, selective, Greek-life and so on). They show as words in the guidebook and the Final Report, and each also has small hidden effects: ±2–12% on applicants, small changes to giving, attrition or costs.
change: Keep the tags as descriptive words but remove their effects. For most colleges the class is capped by class places, not applicants, so the applicant effects rarely change anything.

item: The twelve offices in Founders Hall
why: No goal player opened one in 47 runs; blocking them changed nothing. Seats stay.
now: Founders Hall has free slots that can hold one of twelve administrative offices (career services, financial aid, alumni relations…). Each gives a ±15–20% nudge to one narrow thing.
change: Remove the offices and keep the seats (Provost, Deans and so on). None of the scripted test players opened an office in 47 runs, and blocking them entirely changed nothing measurable.

item: Events whose effect never reaches the map or a seen figure
why: Keep events that land on the map (trees, ivy, a sinkhole, a building) or move a seen number.
now: The event catalogue has hundreds of events (16,400 words). Many have effects that never show anywhere you'd notice: a little cash, a little mood, a little alumni warmth.
change: Keep the events whose effect lands on the map (a tree, ivy, a sinkhole, a building) or moves a number you watch, and trim the rest. This is a writing pass, not a single cut.

item: Negligible edges: faculty quirks' morale, building pairing, a title year's campaign lift, alumni's beauty memory
why: Each is under a point or two on its need.
now: Several effects so small they barely register: professors' quirks nudging morale by up to 3 points on one need, buildings next to each other adding up to 2 points, a title year lifting campaigns 25%, the alumni's memory of a beautiful campus.
change: Remove these effects and the lines that explain them. Each is under a point or two, so the explanation costs more attention than the effect is worth.

item: The board's question (trades 1–2 points between pillars)
why: A weak edge; keep only if it becomes a choice the map shows.
now: Every so often the board writes asking you to favour one pillar over another. Your answer moves 1–2 prestige points between pillars over five years.
change: Keep it only if it becomes a choice the player can see on the map. Otherwise drop the recurring letter.

item: Coach management, team order and athletic scholarships (keep the budget tier)
why: Running no department costs 0–6.5 target points; the championships player spent 176 coach actions on it.
now: In the Athletics tab you hire and fire coaches, drag teams into a priority order, and set athletic scholarships, besides choosing the department's budget level.
change: Remove coach management, team ordering and scholarships, and keep the budget level. Running no department at all cost the test players almost nothing (0–6.5 points, 1–2 places). Having teams matters; managing their staff barely does.

item: The title page that stops the clock
why: Replace with a banner over the map and a pennant on the venue.
now: When a team wins a national title, a fanfare plays and the clock stops on a full-screen Inbox page of text with the bracket and scores.
change: Replace the clock-stopping page with a banner over the map (as when a school becomes distinguished) and a pennant hung on the team's venue for good.

item: The 'prestige dividend' line, the draw-rate slider and the sweep
why: Blocking every Treasury lever cost 0–5 target points; cash piles to $1.7–2.2B.
now: Three money items: a 'prestige dividend' line in the Treasury (about $900 a year per prestige point), a slider for how much of the endowment you draw each year, and a 'sweep' that moves spare cash into the endowment.
change: Remove all three and use a fixed draw. Blocking every Treasury lever cost the test players 0–5 points while cash piled up to about $2 billion. The review suggests late money should buy something visible instead, such as endowed faculty chairs.

item: Reunions (and the Alumni panel down to one line)
why: No goal player held one. Alumni warmth instead feeds word of mouth (card 11).
now: You can hold reunions for alumni, and History has an Alumni panel showing each class's warmth and giving.
change: Remove reunions and shrink the Alumni panel to one line. No test player ever held a reunion. The review suggests alumni warmth should instead feed word of mouth at admissions, where you'd actually see it.

item: Two scores for the campus's looks (beauty and the Campus standing)
why: One score, carried by the map.
now: The game has two separate scores for how good the campus looks: beauty (0–100, from greenery, landmarks, upkeep, quads) and the Campus standing (0–150, from decoration, quads, paths and buildings). The Estate panel shows one and the Build menu shows the other.
change: Merge them into one score. You chose trim; Plan 124 keeps both in the game's maths but shows the player only one figure, with beauty's parts listed under it.

item: Gold as unread, retiring, good-on-the-band, full residence, lab progress and the Build button's permanent outline
why: Gold means only 'selected / do this'.
now: The school's gold colour means about ten things: the selected tab, the main button, 'good' on the dark band, a Distinguished program, a full residence, lab progress, an unread letter, an active project, a professor about to retire, and 'do this'. The Build button also has a gold outline all the time.
change: Make gold mean only 'selected / do this' and give the other meanings other colours (unread becomes cream, retiring becomes red, and so on). You chose trim; Plan 124 removes the three most misleading: retiring, unread and Build's permanent outline.

item: Pulses on developing courses and the ready committee seat; urgent as a pulse
why: The pulse means 'do this' only; the lamps' fill already shows progress.
now: Some things pulse continuously: courses being written in the Curriculum tab, and a free committee seat ('breathing'). An urgent Inbox item also pulses, as does the 'do this' highlight.
change: Keep the pulse for 'do this' only. Stop the always-on pulses for things in progress, since the lamps already fill to show progress, and show urgent as steady red.

item: Background sound cues (tick for departures, candidates, petitions, publications, training)
why: One chime for everything means nothing; give the finished building its own cue.
now: The same short chime plays when a building finishes, a program opens, a milestone is reached, research breaks through, or a demand is met. A 'tick' plays for nine kinds of background news, including both hiring and losing a professor.
change: Make sounds mean one thing each: silence the background ticks, give a finished building its own sound, and stop a departure sounding like a hire. You chose trim; Plan 124 silences a departure, gives a failed demand the 'loss' sound, and silences three background ticks.

item: The 'Guide' button name (clashes with the rankings guide) and 'Distinguished' as a professor's rank
why: Rename the button 'Show me' (or cut it with the walks) and the rank 'Chair'.
now: Two words mean two things each. 'Guide' is both the button that starts a tab's tour and the rankings publication ('#48 in the guide'). 'Distinguished' is both a professor's top rank and a program's top standing.
change: Rename the tour button 'Show me' and the professor rank 'Chair', so each word means one thing.

item: Unicode glyphs among the Lucide icons (map tools ⤓ ⤒ ⌂, school motifs ◆ ⚙ ✦ ❧ ⚗ ✚ ▣)
why: Draw them in the icon set's stroke, or drop the motifs: the school's colour already marks it.
now: Most icons are drawn line icons (the Lucide set). A few are text characters instead: the map tools' ⤓ ⤒ ⌂ for tilt and home, and the school symbols ◆ ⚙ ✦ ❧ ⚗ ✚ ▣ in the Curriculum headers. They look heavier and different.
change: Redraw them to match the other icons, or drop the school symbols since each school's colour already marks it. You chose trim; Plan 124 redraws the map tools' three and leaves the school symbols alone.

item: Seven entrance motions with rises of 10, 12 and 18 px
why: One rise and one fade.
now: Panels, popups, modals, toasts and banners slide in with seven different animations, rising 10, 12 or 18 pixels.
change: Use one rise and one fade everywhere, so things arrive the same way. You chose trim; Plan 124 brings it down to three: a rise, a fade and the banner.

item: The title backdrop's top-down plan and the founding form's flat elevation
why: Three projections in the first minute; prefer the isometric map and hall.
now: In the first minute the player sees three drawing styles: the title screen's top-down turning map, the founding form's flat front view of the hall, and then the game's angled (isometric) view.
change: Use the isometric view on the title screen and the founding form too, so the hall you design is the hall that lands. You chose trim; Plan 124 changes the title screen and keeps the founding form's front view, which the review liked.

item: The RENOVATE_LIBRARY action (no screen dispatches it)
why: Its reducer case is unreachable from the interface.
now: A leftover game action for renovating the library. Nothing in the interface can trigger it any more; the library grows another way now.
change: Delete the unused code. Players won't notice any change.
